title: Allowing both safe and unsafe HTTP methods is security-sensitive
description: Allowing both safe (e.g., GET, HEAD) and unsafe (e.g., POST, PUT, DELETE) HTTP methods on the same endpoint can lead to security vulnerabilities such as Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and unintended data modification. Endpoints should be restricted to only the HTTP methods necessary for their intended function.
message: Endpoints should not allow both safe and unsafe HTTP methods. Restrict HTTP methods to only those required for the endpoint's purpose.
impact: Attackers may exploit endpoints that allow unsafe HTTP methods to perform unauthorized actions, modify data, or bypass security controls.
recommendation: Explicitly specify allowed HTTP methods for each endpoint in your web framework (e.g., Flask, Django). Avoid using default settings that allow all methods. Regularly review and audit routes to ensure only necessary methods are enabled.

noncompliant.description: This endpoint allows both GET (safe) and POST (unsafe) methods, increasing the risk of CSRF and unintended data changes.

compliant.description: This endpoint only allows the POST method, reducing the attack surface and preventing unsafe operations via GET requests.

devsecops.security: Improper HTTP method restrictions can lead to CSRF and unauthorized data modification.
devsecops.automation: Automated security testing should verify that only required HTTP methods are enabled.
devsecops.compliance: Helps meet OWASP and industry best practices for secure web application design.

why_is_this_an_issue: Allowing both safe and unsafe HTTP methods on the same endpoint increases the risk of attacks such as CSRF and can result in unauthorized data changes. Restricting HTTP methods is a fundamental security control.
how_to_fix: Review all endpoints and explicitly define allowed HTTP methods. Use decorators or configuration options in your web framework to restrict methods. Remove any unnecessary or unsafe methods from endpoints.
